sentences.text: Cretoxyrhina was an extinct genus of large shark that lived during the Late Cretaceous, between 100 and 73 million years ago.
The name Cretoxyrhina combines 'creto' for Cretaceous and 'Oxyrhina' from Greek words meaning sharp nose.
Cretoxyrhina teeth are distinguished by a triangular shape, razor-like non-serrated edges, visible tooth necks, and a thick enamel coating.
Cretoxyrhina had dense overlapping placoid scales with U-shaped grooves averaging 45 micrometers in width.
Cretoxyrhina mantelli had a dental structure suited for slicing and dicing prey, using spear-like front teeth to stab and curved rear teeth to cut.
The genus is occasionally known as the ginsu shark.
A Cretoxyrhina skeleton reported to be 20 feet long contained stomach contents of a Xiphactinus and about 150 visible teeth.
The best-preserved specimen FHSM VP-2187 was estimated to be 1.28 meters long and weigh 16.3 kg at birth, doubling its length within 3.3 years.
A 2013 study identified a syntype tooth from England that calculated a maximum length of 8 meters, making it the largest known specimen of C. mantelli.
Louis Agassiz first identified this shark in 1843 based on fossils found in France.
Louis Agassiz reclassified the teeth as a single species in 1843, noting their similarity to species in the now-invalid genus Oxyrhina.
Charles R. Eastman published an analysis of a Cretoxyrhina skeleton in 1894.
In 1958, Leonid Glickman proposed the new genus Cretoxyrhina based on the dental design of O. mantelli.
The shark grew up to 8 meters long and weighed approximately 5000 kilograms.
The powerful jaws, high speed, and large size suggest Cretoxyrhina was a very aggressive predator.
Cretoxyrhina primarily hunted other active predators such as ichthyodectids, plesiosaurs, turtles, mosasaurs, and other sharks.
The fossil record reveals it hunted a variety of marine animals including mosasaurs like Tylosaurus, plesiosaurs like Elasmosaurus and Xiphactinus, and protostegid turtles like Archelon.
Fossil evidence of Cretoxyrhina feeding includes large, deep bite marks and punctures on bones, sometimes with embedded teeth.
Evidence of interspecific interactions exists in the form of bite marks between Cretoxyrhina and large mosasaurs like Tylosaurus, which exceeded 10 meters in length.
Researchers speculate that the shark hunted by lunging at high speeds to inflict powerful blows, relying on strong eyesight.
Hydrodynamic calculations suggest the shark could reach burst speeds of up to 70 kilometers per hour.
Cretoxyrhina mantelli possessed regional endothermy, likely featuring red muscles near the body axis and a rete mirabile system to conserve metabolic heat.
Cretoxyrhina mantelli's partially warm-blooded physiology allowed it to function efficiently in cold environments where fossils have been found.
Although no fossil evidence exists, Cretoxyrhina is inferred to have been ovoviviparous like modern mackerel sharks.
Researchers suggest Cretoxyrhina was an r-selected shark producing many infants to offset high mortality rates in waters with predators like Tylosaurus and Xiphactinus.
Analysis of vertebrae indicates the shark reached sexual maturity at four to five years and had a lifespan of nearly forty years.
The von Bertalanffy growth model estimated the maximum lifespan of C. mantelli to be 38.2 years, at which point it would have exceeded 7 meters in length.
The genus is traditionally placed in the family Cretoxyrhinidae, though some researchers propose it belongs in Alopiidae or Lamnidae.
Cretoxyrhina is traditionally classified within the family Cretoxyrhinidae, which some researchers consider paraphyletic or polyphyletic.
Glickman's 1964 replacement of the type species C. mantelli with Isurus denticulatus is now rejected as an invalid taxonomic amendment.
The earliest fossils of Cretoxyrhina date back to about 107 million years ago and belong to the species C. vraconensis.
Cretoxyrhina had a cosmopolitan distribution with fossils found worldwide, including North America, Europe, Israel, and Kazakhstan.
The shark preferred subtropical to temperate pelagic waters but may have lived in water as cold as 5 degrees Celsius.
A single tooth dated to 70.44 million years old suggests Cretoxyrhina may have survived into the Maastrichtian, though this is debated due to the brackish nature of the deposit.
It is debated whether competition with the giant mosasaur Tylosaurus contributed to the shark's extinction.
